newsitem.title: USA: CBOT panel shocked by USDA winter wheat seedings. [CORRECTED 18:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: CBOT panel shocked by USDA winter wheat seedings. [CORRECTED 18:00 GMT]

text.p: Analysts on a panel sponsored by the Chicago Board of Trade said they were shocked by the low government U.S. winter wheat seedings estimate released early Friday and said wheat futures at the three U.S. wheat futures exchanges should open sharply higher.
"The biggest shocker of the report was the winter wheat acreage number, the lowest since 1978," said Dan Basse, Executive Vice President of Chicago-based analytical firm AgResource Co.

The U.S. Agriculture Department on Friday said U.S. farmers seeded 48.222 million acres of winter wheat last fall for harvest during the early summer of 1997. That seedings tally was sharply below an average of analysts' expectations for 51.4 million acres.

Basse and John Zanutto, Senior Vice President of LFG Futures, Chicago, told reporters following the release early Friday of the government's final 1996 crop production report that all numbers were bullish.
Wheat, corn and soybean futures were expected to open strongly higher, the experts said.

"The precipitous drop in wheat prices (during 1996) caused farmers to shift away from wheat acres," Zanutto said. "The transition from light supplies to ample has taken a shot in the arm here, it has taken an arrow."
"Maybe the biggest factor was the large sorghum crop last year. The harvest was strung out and wheat prices were not that attractive," Basse said.
But the panel said the wheat market, while capturing significant attention, certainly was not the only focal point of the government's crop production and stocks data released Friday morning.
USDA pegged 1996 U.S. soybean production at 2.382 billion bushels, below average expectations for 2.407 billion.

It also lowered the 1996-97 U.S. soybean carryout to 155 million bushels from the previous outlook for 180 (corrects from 210) million and CBOT traders early were calling soybean futures to open from 15 to 20 cents per bushel higher.
"Securing bean supplies over the next few months will be difficult," Zanutto said referring to the tight holding by farmers of the 1996 U.S. soybean crop.

Corn prices also were expected to be strongly higher Friday. USDA pegged 1996 U.S. corn production at 9.293 billion bushels, below average expectations for 9.317 billion. Also, 1996-97 U.S. corn ending stocks estimates were trimmed to 959 million bushels from the previous 1.157 (corrects from 1.107) billion bushels.
